claims.evidence: This is a classic finding from Schultz's work, cited in the introduction.

claims.claim: If a sensory cue reliably predicts reward, dopamine neurons decrease their response to reward, and instead burst to the cue.
claims.source: If a sensory cue reliably predicts reward, however, dopamine neurons decrease their response to reward, and instead burst to the cue.
claims.evidence: This is a classic finding from Schultz's work on reward prediction error.

claims.claim: If an expected reward is omitted, dopamine neurons pause their firing at the time they usually receive reward.
claims.source: Finally, if an expected reward is omitted, dopamine neurons pause their firing at the time they usually receive reward (Hollerman and Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a classic finding from Schultz's work on reward prediction error.

claims.claim: It is thought that the majority of dopamine neurons are inhibited by aversive stimuli.
claims.source: It is thought that the majority of dopamine neurons are inhibited by aversive stimuli (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011; Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1996; Tan et al., 2012; Ungless et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about dopamine neuron responses to aversive stimuli, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: A number of electrophysiological recording studies have reported that dopamine neurons are activated by aversive stimuli both in anesthetized and awake animals.
claims.source: However, a number of electrophysiological recording studies have reported that dopamine neurons are activated by aversive stimuli both in anesthetized (Brischoux et al., 2009; Coizet et al., 2006; Schultz and Romo, 1987) and awake animals (Guarraci and Kapp, 1999; Joshua et al., 2008; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009), although the proportions and locations of aversion-activated neurons differed among these studies.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes findings from multiple cited studies showing activation of dopamine neurons by aversive stimuli.

claims.claim: Roitman et al. (2008) found that dopamine release was increased by sucrose and decreased by quinine.
claims.source: This study found that these stimuli caused opposite responses: dopamine release was increased by sucrose and decreased by quinine (McCutcheon et al., 2012), suggesting that at least the majority of dopamine neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens are inhibited by aversive stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study using cyclic voltammetry.

claims.claim: Matsumoto and Hikosaka (2009) showed that dopamine neurons that are activated by the prediction of aversive stimuli are located in the lateral part of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc).
claims.source: They showed that dopamine neurons that are activated by the prediction of aversive stimuli are located in the lateral part of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), supporting the notion that dopamine subpopulations are spatially segregated (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study about spatial organization of dopamine neurons.

claims.claim: Lerner et al. (2015) showed that SNc neurons projecting to the dorsolateral striatum are activated by aversive stimuli (electric shock) whereas those projecting to the dorsomedial striatum are inhibited.
claims.source: Consistent with this finding, Lerner et al. (2015) showed, using calcium imaging with fiber photometry, that SNc neurons projecting to the dorsolateral striatum are activated by aversive stimuli (electric shock) whereas those projecting to the dorsomedial striatum are inhibited (Lerner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study using calcium imaging.

claims.claim: Fiorillo (2013) concluded that dopamine neurons represent prediction errors with respect to reward but not aversiveness.
claims.source: One influential paper by Fiorillo (2013) concluded that dopamine neurons represent prediction errors with respect to reward but not aversiveness (Fiorillo, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from a cited study that the current manuscript aims to test.

claims.claim: Fiorillo (2013) found that dopamine neurons' responses to aversive outcomes (air puff) were indistinguishable from their responses to neutral outcomes.
claims.source: Recording from non-human primates, Fiorillo used three pieces of evidence to support this claim: First, dopamine neurons' responses to aversive outcomes (air puff) were indistinguishable from their responses to neutral outcomes.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Fiorillo's cited study.

claims.claim: Fiorillo (2013) found that although most dopamine neurons reduced their reward responses when the reward was predicted, their response to aversive events was unaffected by prediction.
claims.source: Second, although most dopamine neurons reduced their reward responses when the reward was predicted, their response to aversive events was unaffected by prediction.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Fiorillo's cited study.

claims.claim: Fiorillo (2013) found that dopamine neurons did not integrate the value of aversive events when combined with rewarding events.
claims.source: Third, dopamine neurons did not integrate the value of aversive events when combined with rewarding events.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Fiorillo's cited study.

claims.claim: Dopamine neurons were mostly recorded from the central and posterior part of the lateral VTA including the parabrachial pigmented nucleus (PBP), parainterfascicular nucleus (PIF) and paranigral nucleus (PN).

claims.claim: Among 26 identified dopamine neurons, 85% (22 neurons) were significantly modulated by the three odors (water, nothing, air puff).
claims.source: Among 26 identified dopamine neurons, 85% (22 neurons) were significantly modulated by these three odors (p<0.05, one-way ANOVA), and 59% (13 of 22 significant neurons) showed the monotonic CS value coding (water > nothing > air puff).

claims.claim: Activation of dopamine neurons alone is sufficient for appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Recent studies using optogenetics have established that activation of dopamine neurons alone is sufficient for appetitive conditioning (Steinberg et al., 2013; Tsai et al., 2009; Witten et al., 2011) whereas suppression is sufficient for aversive conditioning (Chang et al., 2016; Danjo et al., 2014; Ilango et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012), although activation of dopamine neurons that project to the cortex or dopamine neurons in the dorsal raphe has potential to induce aversion and/or other functions (Lammel et al., 2014; Matthews et al., 2016; Popescu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple optogenetic studies cited in the discussion.

claims.claim: Suppression of dopamine neurons is sufficient for aversive conditioning.

claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple optogenetic studies cited in the discussion.

results.result: The study used optogenetic tagging to identify dopamine neurons in the lateral VTA of DAT-Cre mice. A total of 72 optogenetically-identified dopamine neurons were recorded from 176 total VTA neurons across 14 mice, primarily from the parabrachial pigmented nucleus (PBP), parainterfascicular nucleus (PIF), and paranigral nucleus (PN).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 describe the experimental subjects, recording approach, and anatomical localization. The optogenetic identification method is well-established (Cohen et al., 2012), sample sizes are clearly stated, and anatomical reconstruction is provided in figures. This methodological foundation is appropriately documented.

results.result: In the mixed prediction task (low reward context), dopamine neurons showed differential responses to cues predicting different outcomes: excitation to reward-predicting cues and inhibition to aversive-predicting cues. 85% of neurons were significantly modulated by the three odors (water, nothing, air puff), with 59% showing monotonic value coding (water > nothing > air puff).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by data from Figure 2 showing clear differential responses with appropriate statistical tests (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05). The sample size (n=26 neurons) is adequate, and the monotonic coding pattern is quantified. The results are replicated across individual animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

results.result: When a single odor predicted both reward and punishment, dopamine neurons showed intermediate responses compared to cues predicting only reward or only punishment. 89% of neurons were significantly modulated, with 65% showing monotonic value coding (water > water+air puff > air puff), indicating that dopamine neurons integrate values along a one-dimensional axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 demonstrate value integration using the mixed prediction task. The intermediate response to mixed outcome cues (Figure 2F-H) with appropriate statistics (one-way ANOVA, paired t-tests) supports the conclusion. This directly contradicts Fiorillo (2013) and provides strong evidence for integrated value coding. Sample size (n=26) is adequate.

results.result: Dopamine neurons signal prediction errors for aversive events: inhibitory responses to air puff were significantly reduced when predicted versus unpredicted, and omission of predicted air puff slightly but significantly increased firing rates compared to nothing trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 demonstrate aversive prediction error coding with data from Figure 3. Both key signatures of prediction error (reduced response to predicted outcomes and increased response to omitted outcomes) are shown with appropriate statistics (paired t-tests, auROC analysis). The authors acknowledge variability in omission responses, which is appropriately cautious. Sample size (n=38) is adequate.

results.result: The response function to aversive stimuli was preserved across dopamine neurons: neurons strongly inhibited by air puff showed larger prediction-dependent reduction (r=0.69, p=1.9×10⁻⁶), and inhibitory CS responses correlated with prediction-dependent US reduction (r=0.39, p=0.016).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 and C53 demonstrate homogeneity in aversion response function using correlation analyses (Figure 4A-B). The strong correlation (r=0.69) with highly significant p-value indicates preserved response function across neurons, similar to previous findings for reward (Eshel et al., 2016). This suggests functional homogeneity rather than specialized subpopulations for aversion coding.

results.result: There was no correlation between dopamine neurons' responses to unpredicted water and unpredicted air puff, and no clear subpopulations specialized for reward versus aversion were observed in the lateral VTA.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by Figure 4C showing lack of correlation between reward and aversion responses. The scatter plot shows no obvious clustering, and the text states no correlation was found. This suggests independence of reward and aversion response magnitudes, though both can be encoded by the same neurons. Sample size (n=37) is adequate.

results.result: Reward context dramatically affected dopamine responses to aversive cues. In low reward context, all dopamine neurons (12/12) were inhibited by air puff CS, while in high reward context, only 65% showed stronger inhibition to air puff CS than nothing CS (p=0.02). High reward context induced biphasic responses (early excitation, later inhibition), and net responses to air puff CS and nothing CS were no longer significantly different.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 demonstrate context-dependent aversion coding with direct comparison between high and low reward probability tasks (Figure 5). The chi-square test (p=0.02) appropriately compares proportions of neurons showing inhibition. The biphasic response pattern in high reward context is clearly shown. Sample sizes are adequate (n=12 low, n=17 high). This is a key finding explaining discrepancies in prior literature.

results.result: Trial-by-trial dopamine activity correlated with anticipatory eye-blinking behavior in a context-dependent manner. In low reward context, dopamine inhibition was significantly greater in blink trials (p=0.02) and only showed significant inhibition when animals blinked (p=4.3×10⁻⁵). In high reward context, inhibition was greatly reduced even during blinking (p=0.009).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 link neural activity to behavior using concurrent eye-tracking (Figure 6). The correlation between dopamine inhibition and blinking specifically in low reward context is well-documented with appropriate statistics. The dissociation in high reward context (reduced inhibition despite blinking) suggests dopamine signals value rather than directly triggering behavior. Sample sizes and statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: Mice showed anticipatory blinking in 48% of air puff trials but more consistent anticipatory licking in 98% of water trials. Dopamine neurons were excited by reward cues when animals showed anticipatory licking but not when they didn't.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 quantify behavioral responses and their relationship to dopamine activity. The asymmetry between blinking (48%) and licking (98%) is noted, likely reflecting the mild aversiveness of air puff versus high reward value of water. The correlation with licking behavior (Figure 6F) parallels the blinking results, though the authors acknowledge small sample size for no-lick trials.

results.result: In low reward contexts, dopamine neurons were exclusively inhibited by aversive events, expectation reduced responses to both reward and punishment, and dopamine neurons signal value prediction errors (VPEs) integrating reward and aversion in a common currency.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, and C5 summarize the main findings in low reward contexts. These are well-supported by the data showing: (1) consistent inhibition by aversive cues (C24-C27), (2) prediction error coding for both reward and aversion (C32-C34), and (3) value integration (C28-C31). The convergent evidence from multiple experiments strongly supports this integrated VPE model.

results.result: In high reward contexts, dopamine neurons acquired short-latency excitation to aversive events that masked VPE signaling. This excitation compromised monotonic value coding and was not simply a constant offset added to value signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C58, and C59 describe the disruption of value coding in high reward contexts. The biphasic response pattern (C41-C42) and loss of discrimination between aversive and neutral cues (C40) support this conclusion. The observation that this is not a simple additive effect is important for understanding the mechanism. Data from Figure 5 and supplementary analyses support these claims.

results.result: Dopamine inhibition by aversive cues correlated with trial-by-trial variability in aversion-related behaviors in low reward contexts, and similar correlations were observed for reward-related behaviors. Specifically, the degree of inhibition (not excitation) positively correlated with anticipatory eye-blinking.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C61, and C63 establish the behavioral relevance of dopamine signals. The trial-by-trial correlation between inhibition and blinking (Figure 6D) with appropriate statistics supports this. The specificity to inhibition (not excitation) and context-dependence strengthen the interpretation that dopamine signals value rather than motor commands.

results.result: Background claims about dopamine's role in learning and reward prediction error (RPE) theory are established in the field, including that dopamine neurons burst to unexpected rewards, shift responses to predictive cues, and pause when expected rewards are omitted.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C10 summarize well-established prior work on dopamine and RPE, appropriately cited (Schultz et al., 1997; Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; etc.). These provide necessary context for the current study's focus on aversive events. The citations are appropriate and accurate representations of prior work.

results.result: Prior literature shows conflicting results regarding dopamine responses to aversive stimuli: some studies report inhibition while others report activation, with differences potentially related to anatomical location, projection targets, and experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 accurately summarize the conflicting prior literature on dopamine and aversion. The citations are appropriate (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Lerner et al., 2015; etc.). This establishes the motivation for the current study and highlights the importance of optogenetic identification and controlled experimental conditions.

results.result: Fiorillo (2013) concluded that dopamine neurons represent prediction errors for reward but not aversiveness, based on findings that: (1) responses to aversive outcomes were indistinguishable from neutral outcomes, (2) aversive responses were unaffected by prediction, and (3) dopamine neurons did not integrate aversive values with rewards.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 accurately represent Fiorillo's (2013) conclusions, which the current study directly challenges. The citation is appropriate and the summary is fair. This sets up the key contrast with the current findings, particularly regarding value integration (C28-C31) and prediction error coding for aversion (C32-C34).

results.result: Optogenetic studies have established that dopamine neuron activation is sufficient for appetitive conditioning while suppression is sufficient for aversive conditioning, though some dopamine subpopulations may have different functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 accurately summarize optogenetic manipulation studies (Tsai et al., 2009; Witten et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2012; etc.) that establish causal roles for dopamine in learning. The caveat about cortical-projecting neurons is appropriate. These citations support the functional interpretation of the recording data.

results.result: Temporal dynamics analysis revealed that excitation peaks for reward cues occurred earlier than inhibition troughs for aversive cues, and mixed outcome cues showed sequential excitation then inhibition. This suggests different presynaptic sources may convey reward versus aversion information.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 describe temporal dynamics and speculate about circuit mechanisms. While the temporal observations are data-based, the inference about different presynaptic sources (C56) is speculative, though supported by a cited study (Tian et al., 2016). The temporal dynamics are interesting but the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation. The lack of correlation between reward and aversion response magnitudes (C37) provides some support.

results.result: Previous work by Kobayashi and Schultz (2014) found that neutral stimuli excited dopamine neurons more strongly in high- compared to low-reward contexts, consistent with the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 accurately cites prior work showing context-dependent responses to neutral stimuli. This provides important precedent for the current findings about context-dependent responses to aversive stimuli (C38-C42). The citation is appropriate and the connection to current results is valid.

results.result: Oleson et al. (2012) showed that dopamine concentration in ventral striatum increased during active avoidance but decreased during freezing in response to shock-predicting cues, suggesting dopamine responses depend on behavioral strategy.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 accurately represents prior work relating dopamine to behavioral strategies. This is cited in the discussion to contextualize the current findings about dopamine-behavior correlations (C60-C63). The citation is appropriate and provides an alternative framework for interpreting dopamine responses to aversive stimuli.

results.result: Prior studies suggest dopamine neuron diversity based on anatomical location and projection targets, including lateral SNc neurons signaling salience or stable value, ventromedial VTA neurons showing excitation to aversive stimuli, and lateral VTA neurons projecting primarily to ventral and anterior dorsal striatum.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 summarize prior work on dopamine heterogeneity with appropriate citations (Lerner et al., 2015; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Brischoux et al., 2009; Lammel et al., 2008). This contextualizes the current findings and acknowledges that projection targets were not distinguished in this study, which is an appropriate limitation to note.

results.result: Dopamine neurons integrate reward and punishment values along a one-dimensional axis, as demonstrated by intermediate responses to cues predicting both outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C31 state the same key finding about value integration. This is strongly supported by the mixed prediction task data (C28-C30) showing monotonic coding across reward-only, mixed, and punishment-only cues. The statistical evidence (89% modulated, 65% monotonic) with appropriate tests supports this conclusion. This directly contradicts Fiorillo (2013) and is a major contribution.
